report.tagline: A London startup that builds AI that learns to drive from data, and sells it to carmakers and Uber instead of running its own robotaxis.
report.simpleSummary: Wayve teaches cars to drive the way people learn: by watching and practising, not by following hand-written rules or detailed 3D maps. Its single AI model takes in what the car's sensors see and decides how to steer and brake. Wayve does not build cars or run a taxi service. It licenses its software to carmakers like Nissan, Mercedes and Stellantis for driver assistance, and to Uber for robotaxi trials starting in London.

overview.whatItDoes: Wayve builds 'embodied AI' for driving: one neural network trained end to end on large amounts of driving data. Founded in Cambridge, UK in 2017 by Alex Kendall (CEO) and Amar Shah, it is headquartered in London. It sells two products: 'eyes on' hands-free driver assistance for normal cars, and 'eyes off' automated driving for robotaxis and, later, consumer cars.
howItWorks: Wayve collects video and sensor data from fleets of cars, including delivery vans driven by partners.
It trains one large AI model that maps what the car sees straight to driving actions (end-to-end learning).
It does not need high-definition maps, so a car can drive in a new city without months of mapping.
The software works with whatever sensors and chips the carmaker already uses, like Nvidia Drive AGX Thor in its Gen 3 platform.
Carmakers pay to license the software for their cars; Uber will run Wayve-equipped robotaxis on its network.
overview.valueProposition: Carmakers get advanced self-driving features without spending billions building their own, and the same AI can adapt to new cities and car models quickly.

businessModel.summary: Wayve licenses its driving AI to carmakers and platforms rather than building cars or running taxis. It plans to earn a fee per car or per mile driven.

revenueStreams.detail: Fees per vehicle for driver assistance software (Nissan from 2027).
Fees from robotaxi operations on Uber in London and other cities.
Paid engineering work to integrate with each carmaker.

businessModel.unitEconomics: Rough estimate: if a carmaker pays a few hundred dollars per car for driver assistance software, and Wayve is in 1 million cars a year, that is several hundred million dollars a year with low cost per extra car, since software is cheap to copy. The big costs are fixed: training models and engineers. Wayve makes money only if many cars use it; today it is loss-making and funded by investors.

howTheyGetUsers: Deals with carmakers who also invest (Nissan, Mercedes, Stellantis)
Demos in many cities to show the AI generalises
whatBringsUsersBack: Switching cost once software is built into car platforms
growth.moat: Wayve's AI improves with more data, and its hardware-agnostic approach lets it serve many carmakers. Deep, multi-year integrations with carmakers are hard to replace. But rivals with more data, like Tesla, are strong.

pmLessons: You can win by choosing a different business model. Wayve sells software to many carmakers instead of running its own fleet like Waymo.
A different technical bet (learning from data, no HD maps) can make scaling cheaper, but you must prove it is safe.
Partners who invest in you are more likely to buy from you.
B2B products have long cycles: a deal signed in 2026 may only reach customers' cars in 2027.
